title: From Seven Digits to Seventy-Nine
tagline: A student who could hold seven digits, a lab and eighteen months of practice. How to build a routine that keeps all of this alive.
card: A true practice story and a plan: a daily session, a weekly test, a review calendar and a log.
goal: you will design a practice routine with a daily session, a weekly test and a review calendar, and learn why small, regular, focused practice beats long, rare sessions.

left_off.q: How many standard events are there at the memory championships?
Which tool suits the dates event?
Why do some people design a weekly test for themselves?
left_off.a: It shows progress that daily practice alone does not show.

text: In the late 1970s, at a university in the United States, two psychologists, William Chase and Anders Ericsson, were looking for a volunteer for a very dull experiment. They wanted to know how far a person could stretch the memory for digits. They found a student, known in their reports as S.F., who was a keen runner and an ordinary undergraduate.
In the first session he could repeat back about seven digits, which is what most people can do. The psychologists asked him to come back, a few hours a week, to practise.

check.q: How many digits could S.F. remember at the start?

parts.talk: Would you volunteer for an experiment that asked for a few hours a week for over a year? Why or why not?

text: S.F. practised for many weeks. He found that he could do better if he turned the digits into something meaningful. As a runner, he knew a lot about running times, so he made groups of digits into times: 3 4 9 2 was 3 minutes 49.2 seconds, which was almost a world-record mile. He also used dates and ages. He built the groups into larger groups, in a structure.

Slowly the number rose: ten digits, twenty, thirty, forty. After about two hundred and thirty hours of practice, spread over around a year and a half, he could repeat back about seventy-nine digits, from a single hearing. Nobody had thought it possible for an ordinary person.

check.a: He made the digits meaningful (running times, dates) and built them into larger groups, with a lot of regular practice.

parts.talk: What knowledge of your own could you use to make digits meaningful?

text: The experiment taught the psychologists something about practice. S.F.'s memory itself had not changed: when they tested him on letters, he went back to about six or seven. What had grown was a skill, a set of methods tuned to digits. Skill grows with practice, in small regular steps.

The same is true for you. Everything you have learned in the first twenty-eight rooms is a skill. It will fade if you do not use it, and it will grow if you do. This room builds a plan for keeping it alive.

check.a: A skill (methods for digits), not his general memory: with letters he was back to about seven.

parts.talk: Which of your skills got better because you practised a little every day?

words.m: doing something again and again to get better.
a regular way of doing things.
done on purpose, with attention. Deliberate practice.
to keep something in good condition.
a written record of what you did.

source: The study of S.F. is reported by William Chase and Anders Ericsson in the early 1980s. Retold here in our own words.

method.x: A little, often, on purpose. That is the whole secret. The rest is organisation.
A daily session of twenty minutes

head: Minutes
What
Why
rows: Warm-up: walk a palace in your head
Review: test yourself on yesterday's items
New work: one small set (ten items, one chapter, five cards)
Log: write what you did, the time, the mistakes

method.x: Tag each new set with the date you learned it. Review it after one day, three days, a week, two weeks and a month, as in the forgetting curve (room 1). Mark each review in the log.

data.label: Review at one day, three days, a week, two weeks and a month

method.x: Once a week, run a ten-minute test (see room 28): some words, some faces, a few cards or numbers. Record the score. A weekly number is the best way to see progress.
Rules for a routine that lasts

items: Same time and place. A habit grows when it has a cue.
Small and regular. Twenty minutes a day beats three hours once a week.
Make it hard enough. If it is easy, raise the difficulty. If you fail a lot, lower it.
Start with the end in mind. Decide what you want the skill for: exams, talks, names, competition.
Sleep and rest. Memories are consolidated while you sleep.
Teach someone. Explaining a method shows what you have not understood.

method.x: Describe your daily twenty minutes aloud: the warm-up, the review, the new work and the log.

try.title: Design your session
try.prompt: Write your own twenty-minute session: when, where, what warm-up, what review, what new work, how you will log it.
try.model: 7.30 at the kitchen table after coffee. 3 minutes: walk my flat. 5 minutes: test yesterday's ten words. 8 minutes: ten new words. 4 minutes: write the log in my notebook.
checks: There is a time and a place.

try.title: A review calendar
try.prompt: You learned a list today. Write the five dates you will review it, counting from today (day 1, day 3, day 7, day 14, day 30).
try.model: If today is 18 Oct: review on 19 Oct, 21 Oct, 25 Oct, 1 Nov and 17 Nov.
checks: I put them in my calendar.

try.title: Part of the session
try.prompt: Match each part to its purpose.

try.q: A learner studies for four hours on Sunday and nothing else all week. What do you advise?
opts: Twenty-minute sessions on most days instead
try.why: Small, regular practice with review works better.

try.title: Commit
try.prompt: Say aloud the time, the place and the first set you will practise tomorrow.
